title: EchoLeak and the Emergence of CVEs for AI

questions.question: What sequence does naive_copilot follow for the EchoLeak fixture?
options: It retrieves an untrusted email, reads the private MFA inbox, and puts the code in a signed-domain image URL
It trains a new model on the email and deletes the inbox
It blocks retrieval before the model sees any email
It sends the user's prompt to an unrelated public search engine
questions.explanation: The hidden instruction in ATTACKER_EMAIL triggers a lookup in INBOX_PRIVATE, then naive_copilot builds a render_image URL under signed.microsoft.com and places it in rendered_output. The chain crosses retrieval, scope, and output boundaries.

questions.question: Why is EchoLeak called zero-click in the cited attack model?
options: The victim must click an image before any retrieval occurs
The victim need not open the email; normal RAG retrieval supplies its body to Copilot
The attacker needs to install a browser extension first
The attack works only after a user manually forwards the message
questions.explanation: retrieve is called for the ordinary user prompt "summarize my recent emails" and returns the attacker email. No click is needed to make the content part of the agent's context.

questions.question: What does scope_separated_copilot change in the toy defense?
options: It trusts every retrieved email because retrieval is internal
It encrypts the MFA code before putting it in the URL
It labels the retrieved email untrusted, redacts the instruction-shaped suffix, and makes no tool call
It runs the same hidden instruction through a second model
questions.explanation: The defended branch checks email['trust'] and splits at [hidden:, leaving only a summary. The trace therefore shows one retrieved email, an empty tool_calls list, and no exfiltration URL.

questions.question: What are the three independent boundaries in the LLM Scope Violation model?
options: Training, inference, and deployment
Prompt, tokenizer, and context window
Model size, latency, and cost
Retrieval, privileged scope, and output/network exfiltration
questions.explanation: An attacker-controlled retrieval item is only the first step. The model must also reach a privileged scope and send the result across an output boundary; defending one boundary alone leaves another path open.

questions.question: What severity lesson does the EchoLeak disclosure illustrate?
options: An information-disclosure label can understate impact until a concrete MFA-exfiltration proof of concept is demonstrated
CVE scores are determined only by model parameter count
A CSP allowlist guarantees that no AI vulnerability exists
Responsible disclosure prevents all later exploitation
questions.explanation: The lesson describes an initially low assessment that rose to CVSS 9.3 after the practical exfiltration path was shown. AI-specific scope and tool boundaries must be included in severity analysis.

questions.question: Why does the lesson reject input-only classification as an EchoLeak defense?
options: Input classifiers cannot run before retrieval
The payload enters through retrieved content and can trigger privileged actions after the user-input check
A model cannot produce any output after classification
The retrieved instruction can be trusted if it comes from an email
questions.explanation: A filter on the user's text does not necessarily inspect or constrain tool-derived content and side effects. EchoLeak defense requires independent retrieval, scope, and output controls, not only a prompt classifier.
